content: In most Western industrialized nations, second-generation antipsychotics, also known as atypical antipsychotics, are recommended as the first-line pharmacological treatment for individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia. This review specifically evaluates the efficacy and tolerability of aripiprazole, a second-generation antipsychotic, in comparison to other atypical antipsychotics. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of aripiprazole in comparison to other atypical antipsychotics for individuals with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like psychoses. The review included randomized clinical trials (RCTs) that compared oral aripiprazole with oral or parenteral forms of other atypical antipsychotics, including amisulpride, clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, sertindole, ziprasidone, and zotepine. A total of 174 trials involving 17,244 participants were included in the analysis. The overall dropout rate across studies was high, ranging from 30% to 40%, which limits the validity of the findings. The quality of evidence for most outcomes was rated as low or very low. Comparison of Aripiprazole with Clozapine: No significant differences were observed in global state outcomes, as measured by the proportion of participants showing no clinically significant response (29 RCTs, 2132 participants, low-quality evidence). Mental state outcomes, assessed using the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), showed no significant differences (5 RCTs, 426 participants, very low-quality evidence). Rates of study discontinuation for any reason were similar between the two drugs (3 RCTs, 240 participants, very low-quality evidence). Quality of life, measured using the WHO-QOL-100 scale, favored aripiprazole (2 RCTs, 132 participants, very low-quality evidence). No significant differences were found in extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) between the two groups (8 RCTs, 520 participants, very low-quality evidence). No data were available on general functioning or service use. Comparison of Aripiprazole with Quetiapine: No significant differences were found in global state outcomes (12 RCTs, 991 participants, low-quality evidence). Mental state outcomes, assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) for positive symptoms, showed no significant differences (7 RCTs, 583 participants, very low-quality evidence). Rates of study discontinuation for any reason were similar (2 RCTs, 168 participants, very low-quality evidence). No significant differences were observed in general EPS symptoms (4 RCTs, 348 participants, very low-quality evidence). Quality of life outcomes, measured using the WHO-QOL-100 scale, favored aripiprazole (1 RCT, 100 participants, very low-quality evidence). No data were available on general functioning or service use. Comparison of Aripiprazole with Risperidone: No significant differences were observed in global state outcomes (80 RCTs, 6381 participants, low-quality evidence). Rates of study discontinuation for any reason were similar (12 RCTs, 1239 participants, very low-quality evidence). Mental state outcomes, assessed using the BPRS, favored aripiprazole (5 RCTs, 570 participants, very low-quality evidence). Participants receiving risperidone experienced higher rates of EPS (31 RCTs, 2605 participants, low-quality evidence). No data were available on general functioning, quality of life, or service use. Comparison of Aripiprazole with Ziprasidone: No significant differences were observed in global state outcomes (6 RCTs, 442 participants, very low-quality evidence). Mental state outcomes, assessed using the BPRS, showed no significant differences (1 RCT, 247 participants, very low-quality evidence). Rates of study discontinuation for any reason were similar (2 RCTs, 316 participants, very low-quality evidence). Weight gain was significantly greater in participants receiving aripiprazole (3 RCTs, 232 participants, very low-quality evidence). No data were available on general functioning, quality of life, or service use. Comparison of Aripiprazole with Olanzapine: No significant differences were observed in global state outcomes (11 RCTs, 1739 participants, very low-quality evidence). Mental state outcomes, assessed using the PANSS, showed no significant differences (11 RCTs, 1500 participants, very low-quality evidence). Quality of life outcomes, measured using the GQOLI-74 scale, showed no significant differences (1 RCT, 68 participants, very low-quality evidence). More participants receiving aripiprazole discontinued the study early for any reason (9 RCTs, 2331 participants, low-quality evidence). Participants receiving olanzapine experienced significantly more weight gain (9 RCTs, 1538 participants, very low-quality evidence). No data were available on general functioning or service use. Authors' Conclusions: The evidence available for all comparisons is of low or very low quality, making it incomplete and difficult to apply clinically. Aripiprazole is associated with a distinct adverse effect profile, but long-term data are sparse. There is a need for further updates to this review as new data from larger, independent, and pragmatic trials become available.
